brief_summary:
This study compares ways of joining the bowel after surgery for rectal cancer. It aims to find out whether using a single-stapling technique leads to fewer bowel leaks than using a double-stapling technique. It also compares two ways of placing the closing stitch used in the single-stapling technique.

The study will include 124 adults having planned surgery to remove rectal cancer while preserving the anus. After removing the affected part of the rectum, the surgeon joins the remaining bowel. A leak can occur if this join does not heal properly.

Participants will be assigned by chance during surgery to one of two techniques:

Double stapling: the surgeon closes the remaining rectum with a straight stapler, then uses a circular stapler to join the bowel.

Single stapling: the surgeon closes the remaining rectum with a drawstring-like stitch, then uses a circular stapler to join the bowel.

Participants assigned to single stapling will have a second assignment by chance. The surgeon will place the closing stitch either from inside the abdomen or through the anus.

The main outcome is a bowel leak that requires treatment within 30 days after surgery. Researchers will also compare other complications, recovery, findings from the removed cancer tissue, and whether the cancer returns locally during the first year.

Participants will be followed for 12 months after surgery. They will complete questionnaires about bowel function, bowel control, and quality of life at 6 and 12 months.
primary_outcomes: Clinically Significant Anastomotic Leak Within 30 Days
title: Single Versus Double Stapling and Two Purse-String Techniques in Rectal Cancer Surgery

brief_summary:
This quality improvement project aims to improve sleep for older adults during overnight stays in the Emergency Department. Older adults in the ED may experience prolonged stays while awaiting inpatient admission, and this period can involve sleep disruption, immobility, delirium risk, and physiologic stress. The first phase of the project will measure baseline sleep duration and related physiologic patterns among adults aged 70 years or older who are staying overnight in the ED and are admitted, or likely to be admitted, to Medicine.

Participants will be invited to wear a Fitbit Sense 2 device for approximately 24 hours. The device will collect sleep, heart rate, and activity data. Additional information will be collected through patient questionnaires and Epic chart review, including clinical and environmental factors that may affect sleep, such as ED location, overnight vital signs, bloodwork, imaging, medications, interventions, and delirium documentation. Fitbit data will be analyzed in aggregate and will not be used to guide real-time clinical care or flow into Epic.

After baseline sleep patterns and associated factors are better understood, the project will use quality improvement methods, including Plan-Do-Study-Act cycles, to introduce and evaluate practical sleep-improvement strategies through the Seniors Emergency Medicine Centre. Potential interventions may include reducing noise and lighting when clinically appropriate, providing sleep-support items such as earplugs and eye masks, using white noise, improving equipment and alarm management where safe, and considering sleep-promoting medications such as melatonin when appropriate. The primary outcome is total sleep time during the overnight ED stay, measured using Fitbit data. Secondary and balancing measures include patient satisfaction with wearing the Fitbit, delirium episodes, care delays related to sleep interventions, and staff feedback about workflow or device-related disruptions.

This project is intended to inform local improvements in care processes for older adults in the UHN Emergency Department and to support safer, more patient-centered overnight ED care. The QIRC submission identifies the project as a UHN quality improvement project focused on process change, information gathering, and evaluation, with an aim to improve overnight total sleep time for older adults by approximately one hour over six months after baseline measurement.

* What is the maximum tolerated dose (MTD), maximum administered dose (MAD), and recommended dose for expansion (RDE) of MC001?

brief_summary:
Chest wall trauma is a major cause of morbidity among trauma patients. Rib fractures are associated with severe pain, impaired ventilation, reduced cough efficiency, secretion retention, prolonged hospital stay, and increased mortality. Rib fractures are also associated with concomitant thoracic injuries, head, extremity, abdominal, and blunt cardiac injuries.

These patients have poor overall clinical outcomes and are at increased risk for multiple complications.

Thoracic complications of rib fractures are common, including pneumonia, pulmonary effusion, aspiration, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), pulmonary emboli, and atelectasis or lobar collapse.

these complications are important as targeted interventions may enable risk reductions. Effective analgesia is therefore a cornerstone in the management of chest trauma.

Systemic opioids have traditionally been used for pain management; however, their use is associated with respiratory depression, sedation, nausea, vomiting, and impaired pulmonary rehabilitation. Regional anesthesia techniques have emerged as valuable alternatives that provide effective analgesia while minimizing opioid-related adverse effects.

The ultrasound-guided erector spinae plane block (ESPB), first described by Forero, is a fascial plane block in which local anesthetic is deposited deep to the erector spinae muscle adjacent to the transverse process. ESPB has demonstrated efficacy in thoracic surgery, breast surgery, and rib fracture analgesia, improving pain scores and respiratory mechanics.

Magnesium sulfate (MgSO₄) possesses antinociceptive properties through antagonism of N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors and modulation of calcium influx. As an adjuvant to local anesthetics, magnesium sulfate has been shown to prolong analgesia and reduce opioid requirements in various regional anesthesia techniques. Recent ESPB studies and systematic reviews have suggested improved analgesic efficacy when magnesium sulfate is added to local anesthetics.

However, there is currently limited evidence regarding the role of magnesium sulfate as an adjuvant to ESPB specifically in patients with unilateral rib fractures. Therefore, this study aims to investigate whether adding magnesium sulfate to bupivacaine in ESPB improves analgesic outcomes and respiratory recovery in this patient population.
primary_outcomes: Diaphragmatic excursion
title: Magnesium-Enhanced ESPB for Respiratory Recovery and Analgesia in Unilateral Rib Fractures

brief_summary:
This study aimed to evaluate the effects of Tai Chi exercise on cognitive functions, fatigue, and depressive symptoms in individuals with Multiple Sclerosis (MS). MS is a chronic neurological disease characterized by demyelination within the central nervous system and is frequently associated with cognitive, physical, and psychological impairments.

Individuals diagnosed with MS were assigned to either an 8-week Tai Chi exercise program or a home-based Frenkel exercise program. Cognitive functions were assessed using the Brief International Cognitive Assessment for Multiple Sclerosis (BICAMS), which comprises the Symbol Digit Modalities Test (SDMT), California Verbal Learning Test-II (CVLT-II), and Brief Visuospatial Memory Test-Revised (BVMT-R). Fatigue was evaluated using the Fatigue Impact Scale (FIS), while depressive symptoms were assessed using the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI).

The study aimed to investigate the effects of Tai Chi exercise compared with a home-based exercise program on cognitive performance, fatigue, and depressive symptoms in individuals with MS. The findings may contribute to the evidence base for non-pharmacological rehabilitation approaches in MS management.

brief_summary: Running-related injuries (RRI) are commonly reported by all levels of runners, which attenuate participation in running. Current evidence has suggested that RRI mostly occur in lower back and lower extremities, and they can be predicted by biopsychosocial factors. In regard of biomechanical factors, previous studies have found that RRI is related to tendon thickness, lower extremities muscle strength, navicular drop, joint alignment, range of motion, kinetic chain, functional movement, and footwear. Increased training volume and participation in marathon competitions are also associated with increased risk of injuries. Furthermore, recent studies has started to investigate influence of psychological aspects, and found correlations between running performance and risk of injuries and passion, grit, and endurance sports self-efficacy. In addition, social factors, such as, sleep and chronotype, may also affect runners' training schedule and recovery, indirectly influencing occurrence of RRI. However, current evidence on biopsychosocial predictors for RRI is limited. Therefore, this study aims to investigate biopsychosocial predictors for RRI in runners who plan to participate in marathons in six-month time. The study plan to recruit 100 participants and measure running habits, physical activity, passion, grit, endurance sports self-efficacy, sleep quality, and chronotype by questionnaires, and lower extremity tendon thickness, muscle thickness, and cross-sectional area by ultrasonography, and lower extremity muscle strength by hand-held dynamometer, and functional performance and running kinematics. The follow-ups will take place every month for consecutive 6 months after the first measurement, and any RRI occurs during the follow-ups will be recorded. The study is expected to assist in understanding mechanism of RRI, further improving sports prevention and treatment strategies.

brief_summary:
The goal of this double-blind randomized controlled superiority clinical trial is to evaluate whether medical nitrous oxide/oxygen premix (MEOPA), combined with exposure to a personalized traumatic script, can improve symptoms of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in adults with treatment-resistant PTSD related to interpersonal violence.

The main questions it aims to answer are:

1. Does MEOPA combined with traumatic script exposure reduce PTSD symptom severity, as measured by the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale for DSM-5 (CAPS-5), compared with medical air combined with traumatic script exposure?
2. Does MEOPA improve associated symptoms and functioning, including depression, anxiety, dissociation, and functional impairment, while maintaining an acceptable safety profile?

Researchers will compare participants receiving MEOPA plus traumatic script exposure with participants receiving medical air plus traumatic script exposure to determine whether MEOPA enhances the therapeutic effects of trauma-focused re-exposure.

Participants will:

* Attend a screening and baseline assessment visit.
* Complete clinician-administered and self-reported questionnaires assessing PTSD symptoms, depression, anxiety, dissociation, suicidality, and functional impairment.
* Write a personalized traumatic script based on their traumatic experience.
* Be randomized to receive either MEOPA or medical air.
* Undergo four weekly treatment sessions consisting of inhalation of the assigned gas combined with exposure to their personalized traumatic script.
* Attend follow-up visits at 1, 3, 6, and 9 months after treatment for evaluation of efficacy and safety outcomes.
primary_outcomes: Change in PTSD symptom severity measured using the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale for DSM-5 (CAPS-5) until 3 months
title: Medical Nitrous Oxide Combined With Personalized Traumatic Script Exposure for the Treatment of Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder

brief_summary:
Prematurity is associated with a high risk of neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs). The prognosis for moderate and late preterm infants (32 to \<37 weeks of gestational age) is better than that for very preterm infants (\<32 weeks of gestational age).

According to the French National Authority for Health (Haute Autorité de Santé, HAS), moderate and late preterm (MLPT) infants are at moderate risk of NDDs. However, although their risk is lower than that of very preterm infants, it remains significant. Recent research has challenged the misconception that MLPT births are associated with little or no increase in developmental delays compared with full-term births. The risk of NDDs is two to three times higher in these infants than in infants born at term. Prematurity, regardless of its degree, affects the motor and cognitive performance of children born preterm. Impaired neurological development persists at different follow-up ages.

Moderate and late preterm infants account for 85% of all preterm births. Consequently, the number of infants with NDDs is substantial, highlighting the need for appropriate care to limit the impact on the healthcare system.

When an NDD is suspected, the HAS recommends providing parental guidance to help parents initiate activities at home while awaiting the implementation of early intervention. However, these children currently receive no standardised follow-up. The lack of specific assessment of MLPT infants, due to underestimation of their neuromotor risk, leads to delays in care. These delays may result in delayed neuromotor development and potentially long-term sequelae. Yet interventions initiated before discharge from the neonatal unit have the greatest positive impact on the neuromotor development of preterm infants.

Parental education is an effective early intervention strategy. It provides a significant opportunity to improve young children's motor, language, cognitive and socio-emotional development, as well as attachment. It also helps parents develop a better understanding of their infants and promotes parent-infant interactions.

We hypothesise that an early preventive care pathway (PREKINOU) could improve the motor development scores of MLPT infants at 9 months of corrected age.

The objective of the study is to evaluate the effectiveness of an early preventive and educational care pathway (PREKINOU) on the motor development of MLPT infants at 9 months of corrected age (41 weeks ± 14 days), compared with standard care.

This study will include 92 infants born moderately or late preterm. The infants will be randomised into two groups. Infants in the experimental group (n = 46) will follow the PREKINOU pathway in addition to standard care and mandatory medical examinations, both in the maternity unit and after discharge home, until 13 weeks of corrected age (CA).

At 9 months of corrected age (41 weeks ± 14 days), infants in both the experimental and control groups will undergo a blinded assessment using the motor, cognitive and language subscales of the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, Fourth Edition (Bayley-4). The assessment will be conducted by a psychomotor therapist trained in the administration of this scale.

Parents' perceptions of their ability to care for their infants will also be assessed at 9 months of corrected age using the Maternal Perceived Parental Self-Efficacy questionnaire (PMP-SE).

The level of parental engagement in the experimental group will be measured using logbooks. Parental support for the development of infants in both the experimental and control groups will be assessed at 9 months of corrected age using a questionnaire.
primary_outcomes: Motor subscale of the Bayley Scales
title: Evaluation of an Early Preventive and Educational Care Pathway for Moderate and Late Preterm Infants. A Randomized Controlled Study

brief_summary:
Postpartum depression (affecting approximately 15% of women) and childbirth-related post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) (affecting approximately 5%) are major public health concerns due to their frequency and their impact on both maternal and child health. Diagnosis relies on specialized clinical interviews, which are difficult to offer systematically to all women after childbirth. Consequently, self-report screening tools are widely used, particularly the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) for postpartum depression and the Primary Care PTSD Screen for DSM-5 (PC-PTSD-5) for PTSD.

However, these tools were developed and validated in the general population and may be less suitable for certain groups, particularly migrant women, who are at increased risk of postpartum mental health disorders. Their migration experiences are sometimes marked by traumatic events, which may contribute to complex forms of PTSD, and their clinical presentations may differ from those typically observed. Certain culturally specific expressions of psychological distress, dissociative symptoms, or somatic manifestations are not captured by current screening questionnaires.

Furthermore, cultural differences, perceptions of mental health, and language barriers may complicate the psychological assessment of these women and influence their responses to screening tools. These specific factors suggest that existing questionnaires may have insufficient diagnostic performance in some groups of migrant women.

The Psy4Mums project therefore aims to assess the relevance and performance of these screening tools in migrant populations that are particularly vulnerable from psychological, social, and economic perspectives. This evaluation may, if necessary, lead to adaptations in their content, cutoff scores, or methods of administration in order to improve the identification of postpartum mental health disorders. This approach is especially important in French Guiana, where more than half of all women giving birth are migrants.
primary_outcomes: Comparison of PC-PTSD Score with psychiatric evaluation of PTSD
Comparison of EPDS Score with psychiatric evalution of post partum depression
title: Evaluation of the EPDS and PC-PTSD-5 Scales for Screening Postpartum Mental Health Disorders Among Migrant Women.

brief_summary:
This randomized controlled trial aimed to compare the effects of simulation-based training and traditional demonstration-based training on knowledge and practical skills related to percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) care among first-year nursing students.

The study included 40 nursing students who were randomly assigned to two groups: a simulation-based training group (n=20) and a traditional training group (n=20). All participants received four hours of theoretical instruction on PEG care, enteral feeding, and medication administration. The simulation group then participated in a two-hour structured training session using a simulation mannequin and an interactive clinical scenario. The control group received a two-hour traditional demonstration-based laboratory session.

PEG-related knowledge was assessed before training and one week after the practical training sessions using a 25-item knowledge test. Practical skills were evaluated after training through an Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) using a 25-step skills checklist.

The study aimed to determine whether simulation-based training was more effective than traditional demonstration-based training in improving nursing students' knowledge and practical skills related to PEG care.

PEG Care Practical Skill Performance Score
title: Simulation-Based Versus Traditional Training for Percutaneous Endoscopic Gastrostomy Care in Nursing Students

brief_summary:
The goal of this clinical trial is to assess the safety, accuracy and practicality of a new guidance system called Guided Insertion for Tracheostomy (GIFT). The study will involve adults in intensive care who need a tracheostomy as part of their usual treatment.

A tracheostomy is a procedure that creates an opening in the front of the neck to place a breathing tube into the windpipe (trachea). It is commonly performed in intensive care to help people who need prolonged support from a breathing machine.

During the procedure, doctors insert a needle into the windpipe before creating the opening for the breathing tube. Choosing the correct position for the needle is important to avoid injury to nearby structures.

GIFT is a new system that uses electromagnetic technology to help doctors guide the needle towards the intended position. Small sensors allow the system to display the position of the needle in relation to the windpipe in real time. The aim is to help doctors place the needle more accurately and potentially make the procedure safer.

\*\*The main questions this study aims to answer are:\*\*

* Does the System work in the ICU (Is it feasible)
* How accurately can doctors position the needle using GIFT?
* Can GIFT be used safely during tracheostomy procedures in intensive care?
* Does GIFT work reliably during routine clinical procedures?
* Do healthcare professionals find GIFT practical and easy to use?

Participants will:

* Undergo a tracheostomy as part of their usual intensive care treatment.
* Have the GIFT system used to guide needle placement during the procedure, alongside the usual camera guidance used to view the inside of the windpipe.
* Have information about the procedure, any complications and their subsequent recovery collected by the research team.

The study will involve approximately 30-40 participants at Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust.

Our aim is to assess the feasibility of the prototype medical device to guide trained clinicians in bronchoscopy-assisted percutaneous tracheostomy needle insertion, and its integration into the existing tracheostomy workflows in the ICU.

All participants will receive a tracheostomy because their clinical team considers it necessary. The decision to perform the procedure will be made independently of the research.

Researchers will explore a number of safety, usability and performance (accuracy) to evaluate the feasibility of the System. The investigators will measure how close the needle is placed to the intended target and record any problems associated with the procedure or the GIFT system. Investigators will also collect information about participants' recovery in intensive care.

Healthcare professionals involved in the procedures will be invited to complete questionnaires about their experience of using GIFT.

This is an early clinical evaluation of a new medical device. The study is designed to establish whether GIFT can be used accurately, safely and practically in intensive care. It is not designed to prove that GIFT is safer than current tracheostomy techniques.

The findings will help researchers decide whether GIFT should be evaluated in larger clinical trials.

Usability Feasibility: System Usability Scale
Performance Feasibility: Procedural success
title: Guided Insertion Of Tracheostomy Tubes (GIFT): An Early Feasibility Study

brief_summary:
This randomized controlled trial aims to compare the effects of the Graston Technique (instrument-assisted soft tissue mobilization, IASTM) and kinesiology taping on pain intensity, cervical range of motion, and neck-related disability in university students with chronic mechanical neck pain.

A total of 60 students aged 18-25 years with mechanical neck pain lasting at least three months will participate in the study. Participants will be randomly assigned to three groups: Graston Technique, kinesiology taping, or control, with 20 participants in each group.

The Graston group will receive instrument-assisted soft tissue mobilization twice weekly for 12 weeks, while the kinesiology taping group will receive taping once weekly for 12 weeks. Both groups will also receive postural education and static stretching exercises. The control group will receive only postural education and static stretching exercises.

Pain intensity will be assessed using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS), cervical range of motion using a universal goniometer, and neck-related disability using the Neck Disability Index (NDI). All outcomes will be assessed at baseline, week 6, and week 12.

The study aims to determine whether either intervention provides additional benefits beyond postural education and stretching exercises in managing chronic mechanical neck pain among university students.
primary_outcomes: Visual Analog Scale (VAS)
title: Effects of IASTM and Kinesiology Taping on Mechanical Neck Pain in University Students

brief_summary: This is a single-center, open-label, single-arm, prospective, investigator-initiated dose-escalation study to evaluate the safety, tolerability, preliminary efficacy, and cellular kinetics of an in vivo CAR-T cell immunotherapy targeting CD19 sequentially followed by CD22, in patients with relapsed or refractory B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (R/R B-ALL). The investigational product is a targeted lentiviral vector that transduces the patient's endogenous T/NK cells in situ; no leukapheresis, ex vivo manufacturing, or lymphodepleting conditioning is required. Participants receive an intravenous infusion of CD19-targeted in vivo CAR-T on Day 0, followed by an intravenous infusion of CD22-targeted in vivo CAR-T on Day 7. Before the Day 7 infusion, the investigator will assess each participant to determine whether the second infusion should proceed, based on: (i) the proportion of CAR-positive T/NK cells in peripheral blood, which reflects the success of in vivo transduction and early expansion after the first infusion; (ii) the maximum grade and current control of adverse events occurring after the first infusion, including cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS); and (iii) the participant's general condition, including Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status and vital organ function (cardiac, hepatic, renal, pulmonary, and coagulation). The second infusion will be postponed or cancelled if any of these assessments indicates that the risk outweighs the benefit, for example grade \>=3 CRS or grade \>=2 ICANS that has not resolved to grade \<=1, or investigator-judged deterioration in organ function. Dose escalation follows a traditional 3+3 design with planned dose levels of 1×10\^9, 3×10\^9, and 6×10\^9 transducing units (TU), guided by dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs) assessed during Days 0-28; higher dose levels may be explored if the maximum tolerated dose is not reached. Treatment-emergent adverse events and serious adverse events, including CRS, immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS), hematologic toxicity, and organ toxicity, will be assessed. Preliminary antitumor activity will be evaluated by objective response rate (ORR), overall survival (OS), and progression-free survival (PFS), and the expansion and persistence of in vivo-generated CAR-T cells in peripheral blood will also be evaluated.
interventions: CD19-Targeted In Vivo CAR-T Injection (first infusion, Day 0); CD22 -Targeted In Vivo CAR-T Injection (second infusion, Day 7)

Participants will be randomly assigned to three groups: the virtual reality group, the conventional hand massage group, and the control group. Pain levels, anxiety levels, satisfaction levels, and physiological parameters will be assessed both before and after the procedure. brief_summary: Metastatic clear-cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) is sensitive to therapy with lenvatinib and pembrolizumab. The CLEAR trial demonstrated positive outcomes even in patients with a low tumor burden. In a subset of patients with metastatic ccRCC, the presence of a low tumor burden suggests that incorporating stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) into systemic therapy could be a strategy to enhance the anti-tumor response, while maintaining an acceptable toxicity profile. This study evaluates the contribution of SBRT in a subgroup of patients who have achieved stable disease while receiving lenvatinib and pembrolizumab.

brief_summary: Lupus nephritis (LN) is a major cause of renal morbidity in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Conventional clinical, renal, and serological parameters may not fully distinguish patients with renal involvement from those with SLE without LN. This cross-sectional observational study aims to evaluate a predefined panel of eight molecular biomarkers and determine their ability to discriminate between patients with established SLE with and without LN. The panel includes the non-coding RNA markers MALAT1, GAS5, miR-155, and miR-223; the inflammatory biomarkers interferon-beta (IFN-β), lipocalin-2 (LCN2), and interleukin-23 (IL-23); and the tissue-remodeling biomarker matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9). The study will also assess associations between these biomarkers and conventional clinical and laboratory parameters, disease activity, cumulative organ damage, and available renal histopathological findings. The discriminatory performance of conventional clinical assessment, the molecular biomarker panel, and their integrated combination will be evaluated.
primary_outcomes: Discriminatory performance of the predefined molecular biomarker panel for distinguishing SLE patients with established LN from those without LN
title: Molecular Biomarkers for Discriminating Lupus Nephritis in SLE

brief_summary:
One out of six people with HIV (PWH) in the U.S. are incarcerated annually; two-thirds of individuals who are incarcerated meet criteria for substance use disorder (SUD) and many more in carceral settings have risk factors for HIV. Ending the U.S. HIV epidemic hinges on linking and engaging people with criminal legal system involvement (PCLSI) with HIV or related risk factors, especially those with SUDs, to optimize antiretroviral therapy (ART) and pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) uptake and adherence.

In this study, the investigator team will pursue Aim 1 (R33): Test the DEST2nation model in a multisite randomized control trial; and Aim 2 (R33): Estimate the cost of implementing and sustaining a decentralized, status neutral model and estimate its economic value from healthcare sector, state-policymaker, and societal perspectives.

Proportion of Participants without HIV who Initiate PrEP (From enrollment through 12 months post-enrollment)
title: Decentralized, Status Neutral, Stakeholder-engaged, Post-incarceration Intervention for People Living With and at Risk for HIV

brief_summary:
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a long-term condition that can increase the risk of cardiovascular diseases, such as heart attacks and strokes. People with CKD often have other health conditions and take several medications, which can make following treatment plans challenging. Clinical pharmacists may help these patients by reviewing their medications, providing education, and supporting medication adherence and cardiovascular risk management.

This study evaluated the impact of a clinical pharmacist-led pharmaceutical care program on cardiovascular risk, medication adherence, and quality of life in hospitalized adults with CKD.

The study was conducted at a research and training hospital in Istanbul, Türkiye, with a planned six-month follow-up. A total of 150 patients were initially enrolled and assigned to either an intervention group or a control group. Due to deaths, withdrawal from the study, and loss to follow-up, 101 patients were included in the final analysis.

Patients in the control group received standard medical care. Patients in the intervention group received additional pharmaceutical care from a clinical pharmacist, including medication review, education about CKD and cardiovascular risk factors, counseling on medication adherence and lifestyle changes, and follow-up counseling.

The study assessed cardiovascular risk using a Framingham-based risk model. Medication adherence and health-related quality of life were evaluated using standardized questionnaires. Medication regimen complexity and relevant clinical measurements were also assessed.

The findings showed that cardiovascular risk scores decreased in both groups during the study period. Medication adherence increased in both groups, from 59.2% to 75.5% in the control group and from 75.0% to 88.5% in the intervention group. However, the difference in medication adherence between the groups at follow-up was not statistically significant. Quality-of-life scores were significantly higher in the intervention group at both baseline and follow-up. A weak negative correlation was observed between medication regimen complexity and quality of life, indicating that greater medication complexity was associated with lower quality-of-life scores.

Overall, the findings suggest that clinical pharmacist-led pharmaceutical care may support medication management in patients with CKD. However, the study did not demonstrate statistically significant differences between groups in medication adherence or cardiovascular risk outcomes. Further studies with larger samples and adequate follow-up are needed to clarify the effects of pharmacist-led interventions in this population.
primary_outcomes: Change in cardiovascular risk score from baseline to 6 months
title: Clinical Pharmacist-Led Cardiovascular Risk Assessment in Patients With Chronic Kidney Disease (CRICKD)

brief_summary:
Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is one of the most serious and frequent healthcare-associated infections occurring in premature and low-birth-weight infants in neonatal intensive care units. The literature on VAP prevention strongly indicates that a "care bundle" approach is among the most effective methods for reducing the incidence of this infection.

The objective of this research is to determine the impact of a simulation-based intervention-structured around the "H-ER-O-S care bundle" designed to prevent the development of VAP-on the knowledge, skills, self-efficacy/competence, self-confidence, and satisfaction levels of final-year nursing students.

This study will employ a pretest-posttest experimental design and will be conducted at the Lokman Hekim University Vital Simulation Center, involving 34 final-year nursing students.

As part of the pretest and posttest assessments, students will complete the "Self-Efficacy/Competence Scale", the "Student Satisfaction and Self-Confidence in Learning Scale", and "VAP Test". During the simulation, the students' acquisition of the relevant skills will be evaluated and scored using the "H-ER-O-S Care Bundle Checklist." Data will be recorded anonymously in the SPSS software.
primary_outcomes: Knowledge of VAP Prevention
Students' Self-Efficacy/competence
Student Satisfaction with Learning and Self-Confidence in Learning
Performance in Applying the H-ER-O-S VAP Prevention Care Bundle
title: The Effect of Simulation-Based Training on the a Care Bundle to VIP

brief_summary:
The goal of this clinical trial is to learn whether the mSOFA-Kit, a decision support system that calculates the modified Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (mSOFA) score on scene, improves the outcomes of adults attended by Advanced Life Support Units (USVA) for a potentially critical condition.

The main question it aims to answer is: does systematic on-scene stratification of multiorgan risk with the mSOFA-Kit reduce the 2-day composite adverse outcome (all-cause mortality, in-hospital cardiac arrest, admission to a level 2 or 3 ICU, invasive mechanical ventilation or renal replacement therapy) compared with the standard XABCDE assessment?

Researchers will compare USVAs using the mSOFA-Kit with a visible score (intervention arm) with USVAs applying standard XABCDE care with a blinded mSOFA score (control arm). Ambulance units, not individual patients, are randomly assigned to each arm. In both arms, a small venous blood sample, obtained from the peripheral venous catheter already placed for clinical care, is analyzed on scene with a point-of-care analyzer.

Participants will:

* receive the usual prehospital care of their emergency service;
* have their on-scene data and their hospital outcomes recorded;
* be followed up to 90 days through medical records and death registries.
primary_outcomes: Composite adverse outcome at 2 days
title: Prehospital mSOFA-Kit Decision Support for the Detection of Multiple Organ Failure

brief_summary:
The goal of this clinical trial is to investigate if taking Oral B-Complex Vitamin (B6, B9 and B12) can help prevent low anterior resection syndrome (LARS) in rectal cancer patients with hyperhomocysteinemia after sphincter-preserving surgery for rectal cancer. LARS is a group of bowel problems that can occur after rectal cancer surgery, including frequent bowel movements, an urgent need to have a bowel movement, constipation, and loss of bowel control.

Our previous research suggests that hyperhomocysteinemia increased the occurrence of LARS. Folic acid, vitamin B6 and vitamin B12 are a safe, widely used way to treat hyperhomocysteinemia.

The main questions this study aims to answer are:

* Does taking Oral B-Complex Vitamin (B6, B9 and B12) lower the rate of LARS 6 months after surgery?
* How does this treatment affect internal anal sphincter (IAS) function?

Researchers will compare Oral B-Complex Vitamin (B6, B9 and B12) with a placebo (a look-alike tablet that contains no vitamins) to see if Oral B-Complex Vitamin (B6, B9 and B12) can help prevent LARS.

Participants will:

* Take B-Complex Vitamin (B6, B9 and B12) every day for 6 months
* Visit the clinic twice ( 3 months and 6 months after surgery) for checkups and tests
* Complete the LARS score questionnaire 6 months after surgery
interventions: Oral B-Complex Vitamin (B6, B9 and B12)
primary_outcomes: Incidence of Low Anterior Resection Syndrome (LARS)
title: Oral B-Complex Vitamin (B6, B9 and B12) Prevents Low Anterior Resection Syndrome in Rectal Cancer Patients With Hyperhomocysteinemia

brief_summary:
Instrument-assisted soft tissue mobilization (IASTM) is a technique commonly used in sports medicine to reduce muscle tightness and improve range of motion. The technique involves using a handheld instrument, typically made of metal, to apply pressure and massage soft tissues. The instrument allows clinicians to target specific areas while reducing stress on their hands. Previous research has demonstrated that IASTM may improve range of motion and reduce muscle tightness. However, little is known about how the amount of force applied during treatment influences these outcomes. This study aims to investigate the effects of different IASTM treatment forces on calf muscle stiffness and ankle dorsiflexion (the movement of the foot upward toward the shin). Participants will receive either low-force IASTM (0-5 N), high-force IASTM (10-15 N), or no treatment depending on what group they are assigned to. Treatment force will be monitored using a sensor attached to the IASTM instrument (Figure 1). Changes in tissue stiffness will be assessed using the MyotonPRO, a handheld device that measures the mechanical properties of muscles and other soft tissues. Changes in ankle dorsiflexion will be evaluated using clinical movement tests and motion capture analysis.

The findings may help researchers and clinicians better understand how different IASTM treatment protocols influence tissue stiffness and ankle mobility, potentially contributing to more standardized treatment recommendations.
conditions: Range of Motion, Articular, Ankle Joint
primary_outcomes: Change in Weight Bearing Ankle Dorsiflexion Range of Motion
Change in Dynamic Stiffness of the Calf Muscles, Achilles Tendon, and Plantar Fascia
title: Effects of Different Instrument Assisted Soft Tissue Mobilization Force Applications on Ankle Stiffness and Dorsiflexion

brief_summary:
The goal of this clinical trial is to learn if platelet-rich plasma (PRP) made from the patient's own blood helps broken jaw bones heal faster and stronger in adults with fractures of the upper jaw (maxilla) or lower jaw (mandible).

The main questions it aims to answer are:

* Does adding PRP during fracture surgery increase bone density at the fracture site at 6 months compared with surgery alone?
* Is the effect of PRP on bone healing similar in upper jaw and lower jaw fractures?

Researchers will compare patients who receive standard fracture fixation with titanium plates plus PRP to patients who receive the same fixation without PRP, to see if PRP improves bone healing.

Participants will:

* Give a small blood sample (12 ml) before surgery, from which PRP will be prepared (PRP group only)
* Undergo surgery under general anaesthesia to fix the fracture with two titanium plates and screws
* Take antibiotics and anti-inflammatory medicine for one week after surgery
* Return for check-ups and a CBCT (3D dental X-ray) scan at 1 week, 3 months, and 6 months after surgery to measure bone healing
interventions: Open Reduction and Internal Fixation With Titanium Miniplates
lead_sponsor: CMH Lahore Medical College and Institute of Dentistry
primary_outcomes: Bone Density at the Fracture Site
title: Platelet-Rich Plasma for Bone Healing in Maxillary and Mandibular Fractures

brief_summary:
The goal of this observational study is to estimate how common high-risk human papillomavirus (hrHPV) infection is in women aged 50 and older in urban Ethiopia, and which HPV types are present. It will also compare how accurately hrHPV testing alone, or combined with a Pap smear (cytology), identifies serious precancerious changes of the cervix (called CIN2 or worse). A biopsy (a small tissue sample from the cervix) will confirm these changes.

The main questions it aims to answer are:

1. How common is hrHPV infection in women aged 50 and older, and which HPV types are most common?
2. How accurately does hrHPV testing alone, or combined with a Pap smear, identify biopsy-confirmed CIN2 or worse in these women?

After a positive hrHPV result, some women need a follow-up exam of the cervix (colposcopy). Researchers will compare two ways to decide who gets this exam:

Strategy A: All women with a positive hrHPV result get a follow-up exam. Strategy B: Only women with a positive hrHPV result and an abnormal Pap smear get a follow-up exam.

Researchers will apply both strategies to the same group of participants. Participants are not placed in different groups. Researchers will compare how many cases of CIN2 or worse each strategy finds, and how many cases Strategy B misses. They will also compare how many follow-up exams each strategy needs to find one case, how many exams find no CIN2 or worse, and how many exams are needed for every 1,000 women screened.

Participants will:

* Collect their own hrHPV sample with a self-sampling brush
* Answer questions about their health and background, such as age, marital status, number of births, smoking, and past screening
* If their hrHPV result is positive and they agree to more testing, have a Pap smear, a follow-up exam (colposcopy), and a biopsy

This study is exploratory. Its results will help inform cervical cancer screening for women aged 50 and older in Ethiopia.
primary_outcomes: Prevalence of high-risk HPV infection and genotype distribution in women aged 50 and older
Diagnostic accuracy of cytology against biopsy-confirmed CIN2+ in hrHPV-positive women
title: High-risk HPV Testing With Pap Smear Triage for Cervical Cancer Screening in Women Aged 50 and Older in Ethiopia

brief_summary:
This prospective, three-arm, randomized controlled trial aims to investigate the effects of diaphragmatic Kinesio taping applied in addition to pulmonary rehabilitation on diaphragm muscle thickness and function in intensive care unit (ICU) patients.

A total of 48 patients admitted to the ICU due to respiratory distress will be recruited and randomly assigned to three groups: pulmonary rehabilitation combined with diaphragmatic Kinesio taping, pulmonary rehabilitation alone, and a control group receiving routine patient education. The interventions will be administered over a three-day period.

Diaphragm muscle thickness during inspiration and expiration, diaphragm excursion, and diaphragm thickening fraction will be assessed using ultrasonography at baseline and after the intervention period. Cough-related quality of life, anxiety, and depression will also be evaluated using validated questionnaires.

The study aims to determine whether adding diaphragmatic Kinesio taping to pulmonary rehabilitation provides additional benefits in preserving diaphragm muscle thickness and function in critically ill patients.
primary_outcomes: Change in Diaphragm Muscle Thickness During Inspiration
Change in Diaphragm Muscle Thickness During Expiration

brief_summary: This is a single-center, open-label, single-arm, investigator-initiated clinical study to evaluate the safety, tolerability, and preliminary efficacy of SL4903, a BCMA/GPRC5D dual-target autologous CAR-T cell injection, in patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma (R/R MM) whose clonal plasma cells are positive for BCMA and/or GPRC5D. After leukapheresis, participants receive lymphodepleting conditioning (fludarabine 30 mg/m\^2/day plus cyclophosphamide 500 mg/m\^2/day on Days -5 to -3), followed by a single intravenous infusion of SL4903 at a dose of 1×10\^6 CAR-positive cells/kg; bridging therapy (e.g., immunomodulatory drugs or anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody) is permitted between leukapheresis and conditioning at the investigator's discretion. Treatment-emergent adverse events, including cytokine release syndrome (CRS), neurotoxicity, hematologic toxicity, and organ toxicity, will be assessed within 3 months after infusion. Preliminary antitumor activity will be evaluated according to the 2016 International Myeloma Working Group (IMWG) criteria, including objective response rate (ORR), complete response rate (CRR), time to response (TTR), duration of response (DOR), progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), and measurable residual disease (MRD) negativity rate. Pharmacokinetics (Cmax, Tmax, persistence, and AUCd0-28 of CAR-T cells in peripheral blood by flow cytometry and qPCR) and pharmacodynamics (peripheral blood plasma cell proportion and cytokine levels) will also be evaluated. Participants will be followed for safety and efficacy for up to 2 years after cell therapy.
interventions: SL4903 Injection (BCMA/GPRC5D Dual-Target Autologous CAR-T Cell Injection)
primary_outcomes: Adverse Events
Cytokine Release Syndrome
Immune Effector Cell-associated Neurotoxicity Syndrome
title: BCMA/GPRC5D Dual-Target CAR-T Cell Immunotherapy for Relapsed/Refractory Multiple Myeloma

brief_summary:
The goal of this pilot randomized study is to learn whether a dissemination campaign co-designed with a community advisory board helps caregivers of children with anxiety and related disorders seek exposure therapy, compared with standard information. Participants are caregivers of children ages 4 to 18 with current anxiety, OCD, or traumatic stress symptoms.

The main questions it aims to answer are:

Does the dissemination campaign improve caregivers' knowledge of exposure therapy, attitudes toward it, perceived norms about seeking it, and confidence that they can find an exposure therapist, compared with dissemination-as-usual?

Does the dissemination campaign increase caregivers' intentions to seek exposure therapy for their child, compared with dissemination-as-usual?

Researchers will compare the dissemination campaign to dissemination-as-usual, which is links to professional organization websites and advice to contact their insurance company or search an online therapist directory.

Participants will:

* Complete an online survey about their help-seeking intentions, knowledge, attitudes, norms, and confidence
* Be randomly assigned to review either the dissemination campaign or dissemination-as-usual materials for at least 10 minutes
* Complete the same survey again right after reviewing the materials
* Possibly be invited to a 15-minute phone interview 2 months later about whether they sought treatment for their child and what barriers they faced
primary_outcomes: Caregiver Self-Efficacy for Seeking Exposure Therapy
Caregiver Attitudes Toward Exposure Therapy
Perceived Norms for Seeking Exposure Therapy
title: Project Raising Exposure Awareness for Caregiver Help-Seeking

brief_summary: Anhedonia, a reduction in motivation and in the ability to feel positive emotions, is widespread among Veterans across a range of psychiatric disorders. This impairment is associated with poorer psychosocial functioning and is resistant to first-line medication and psychotherapy treatments. However, interventions to improve anhedonia are sorely lacking. Reward learning supports motivation to seek rewards, and this mechanism can be enhanced by engaging in reward exploration. Our preliminary findings suggest that this approach can help improve reward responsiveness and positive mood among depressed and anxious individuals. Thus, the proposed research will test the preliminary efficacy of a computerized reward learning training in improving reward sensitivity and reducing anhedonia in Veterans. This new intervention could offer a novel remotely accessible treatment and help enhance the efficacy of existing evidence-based treatments for depression and other psychiatric conditions in Veterans.
lead_sponsor: VA Office of Research and Development
primary_outcomes: Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale (SHAPS)
Reward Maximization
Neural Activation to Reward Prediction Errors (RPEs)
title: Neurocomputational Training to Improve Reward Responsiveness in Veterans With Anhedonia

brief_summary:
The PLaNT 2 study will test whether giving breathing support soon after birth can help late preterm babies born by cesarean section (C-section). The goal is to lower breathing problems and the need for admission to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU).

Late preterm babies are born a few weeks before their due date. They have a higher risk of breathing problems after birth, especially after a C-section. A recent international pilot study showed promising results with early breathing support in these babies. A larger study is now needed to find out if this approach works.

Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is a common form of breathing support for newborns. It provides gentle air pressure through a mask or nasal prongs. CPAP is usually given after a baby develops breathing problems. PLaNT 2 will test giving CPAP shortly after birth, before breathing problems develop.

The study will include 300 babies born by C-section at 35 to 36 weeks of pregnancy. Babies who are breathing on their own within 5 minutes after birth may take part. The study will randomly assign babies to one of two groups:

* One group will receive 20 minutes of CPAP shortly after birth.
* The other group will receive the hospital's usual care. Babies in either group can receive CPAP or other breathing support later if they need it.

The main question is whether early CPAP lowers the number of babies admitted to the NICU for breathing support. Researchers will also look at the need for breathing support after birth. They will study parental stress, bonding between mothers and babies, and exclusive breastfeeding.

If this approach works, it could lower breathing problems and unnecessary NICU admissions. This could allow more babies to stay with their families. CPAP is already available in many hospitals, so this approach could be used in different health care settings around the world. It may also support early bonding, breastfeeding, and family-centered newborn care.
primary_outcomes: Proportion of NICU admissions for respiratory support.
title: Prophylactic CPAP for Late Preterm Infants Born by C-Section to Reduce NICU Admission

brief_summary:
This study is open to adults with advanced cancer who received obrixtamig (BI 764532) in one of several previous studies and benefited from treatment. The goal of this study is to find out how well participants who received obrixtamig in a previous study tolerate obrixtamig. Obrixtamig is an antibody-like molecule that may help the immune system fight cancer.

Participants in this study continue receiving obrixtamig and any other study or standard of care anti-cancer medicines they received in their previous study at the same doses and following the same treatment schedule. Treatments are given in 3-week cycles as infusions into a vein.

Participants can stay in the study as long as they benefit from treatment and can tolerate it. During this time, they visit the study site regularly. During the visits, study doctors check participants' health and take note of any unwanted effects.
primary_outcomes: Occurrence of treatment-emergent adverse events ( AEs) during the on-treatment period.
title: A Study to Test Obrixtamig Treatment in People With Different Types of Advanced Cancer Who Took Part in a Previous Study With Obrixtamig

brief_summary:
The INPACT study investigates whether a structured program combining physical exercise, nutritional support, and breathing exercises can improve physical fitness and recovery in patients undergoing liver surgery for cancer.

Approximately 103 adult patients with primary liver cancer or liver metastases who are scheduled for liver resection will participate. Participants will be randomly assigned to one of two groups. The control group will receive usual care, including general advice on maintaining physical activity and a healthy diet. The intervention group will follow a structured prehabilitation and rehabilitation program consisting of supervised and home-based exercise, nutritional support including protein supplementation, and daily breathing exercises.

The program starts approximately four weeks before surgery and continues after surgery during the rehabilitation period. Both groups will undergo assessments of physical fitness, muscle strength, nutritional status, quality of life, and other health outcomes at several time points before and after surgery.

The primary aim of the study is to determine whether the multimodal prehabilitation program improves patients' functional capacity before surgery. The study will also evaluate physical performance, nutritional status, quality of life, postoperative recovery and complications, safety, and adherence to the program.
primary_outcomes: Functional capacity measured by the 6-Minute Walk Test (6MWT)
title: INPACT: Implementation of Nutritional Support and Physical Activity During Cancer Treatment

brief_summary: Real-world evidence indicates that deep sedation is the predominant anesthesia strategy for pulsed field ablation (PFA) in most European centers, whereas general anesthesia remains the standard of care in China. Given disparities in anesthesiologist availability and fundamental differences in healthcare system infrastructure and workflow organization, establishing an electrophysiologist-led deep sedation pathway has the potential to streamline PFA procedural logistics, enhance perioperative patient comfort, and facilitate the standardized, scalable, and sustainable implementation of this novel technology. This study aims to determine whether pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) performed with PFA under a remimazolam-based deep sedation protocol is non-inferior to PVI under general anesthesia in terms of both safety and efficacy among patients with atrial fibrillation (AF).

primary_outcomes: Incidence of the composite failure events, including clinical hypoxemia, clinical hypotension, and anesthesia failure.
title: Pulsed Field Ablation for Atrial Fibrillation Under General Anesthesia Versus Remimazolam-based Deep Sedation

brief_summary:
Adults with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)-a neurodevelopmental condition affecting focus, impulse control, and activity levels-often face poor quality of life, emotion management difficulties, and interpersonal challenges. While medication helps core symptoms, it is not always tolerated or fully effective for emotional dysregulation. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends psychological therapies as secondary options, but lacks sufficient evidence to endorse a specific intervention.

The MOPAD study tests whether an introductory Mentalization-Based Treatment (iMBT)-a psychological therapy helping people understand their own and others' mental states-can be delivered in a group format. MBT successfully improves mood and relationship issues in other conditions, offering potential non-drug benefits for adults with ADHD.

This non-randomised interventional feasibility study will recruit 16 adults with diagnosed ADHD. Participants will undertake a 12-week intervention of weekly 100-105 minute group iMBT sessions. Before and after the treatment, participants will complete standardized questionnaires assessing ADHD symptoms, quality of life, emotion regulation, impulsivity, and mentalizing capacity (e.g., ASRS v1.1, CAARS-2, AAQoL, DERS-18, UPPS, MENT-S, RFQ-8), alongside post-study qualitative interviews to share their experiences.

Eligible participants are adults with ADHD recruited from NHS clinical sites. Primary goals are evaluating recruitment (target: 11 participants), retention (target: 70%), safety, therapy fidelity, and patient acceptability. Secondary goals include evaluating clinician feedback and gathering resource data to calculate sample size requirements for a future full-scale trial.
conditions: ADHD - Attention Deficit Disorder With Hyperactivity
interventions: The MOPAD study tests whether an introductory Mentalization-Based Treatment (iMBT)

brief_summary:
During prolonged fasting, the body shifts from using glucose toward using fat as its main energy source. At the same time, skeletal muscle becomes less sensitive to insulin, a hormone that helps regulate blood glucose levels. Although this response is a normal adaptation to fasting, the mechanisms responsible for it are not fully understood.

The DELIVER study aims to investigate how changes in fat metabolism, communication between tissues, and liver energy metabolism contribute to reduced insulin sensitivity during prolonged fasting.

In this randomized crossover study, 18 healthy adults will complete two conditions in random order: a 60-hour fasting period and a control condition involving a standard overnight fast. The conditions will be separated by at least four weeks.

During both conditions, researchers will assess insulin sensitivity, energy metabolism, and fat metabolism using blood and urine samples, magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS), measurements of energy expenditure, and small samples of skeletal muscle and abdominal fat tissue (biopsies). Insulin sensitivity will be measured using a hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp, a procedure in which insulin and glucose are administered intravenously while blood glucose levels are closely monitored.

By comparing the two conditions, the study aims to improve understanding of how the body adapts to fasting and whether some of the mechanisms involved resemble those observed in insulin resistance associated with obesity and type 2 diabetes.
primary_outcomes: Skeletal muscle plasma membrane sn-1,2-diacylglycerol content
title: Mechanisms of Fasting-Induced Insulin Resistance

brief_summary:
The goal of this clinical trial is to learn if a very-low-field MRI scanner (0.064 Tesla), combined with artificial intelligence (AI) image enhancement, can accurately diagnose acute ischemic stroke in adults with suspected stroke. Healthy adult volunteers are also included to optimize image quality. The main questions it aims to answer are:

How accurately does AI-enhanced very-low-field MRI detect ischemic stroke (sensitivity and specificity) compared with standard high-field MRI (3 Tesla)? Does AI enhancement improve diagnostic performance compared with very-low-field MRI images without AI?

Researchers will compare very-low-field MRI images, with and without AI enhancement, to the 3 Tesla MRI performed as part of routine care. Two neuroradiologists will read the images independently, without knowing the results of the other scan.

This study has three parts:

Part 1: healthy volunteers (30 participants). Participants will undergo one 3 Tesla MRI and one very-low-field MRI on the same day (45 minutes maximum).

Part 2: patients with recent stroke, 1 to 7 days after onset (40 participants). Participants will undergo one very-low-field MRI within 6 hours of their routine 3 Tesla MRI.

Part 3: patients with suspected stroke within the last 24 hours (160 participants). Participants will undergo one very-low-field MRI (about 30 minutes) within 4 hours of their routine 3 Tesla MRI, after any emergency treatment. About half will have a second very-low-field MRI around 24 hours later.
primary_outcomes: Sensitivity of AI-enhanced very-low-field MRI for the diagnosis of acute ischemic stroke
Specificity of AI-enhanced very-low-field MRI for the diagnosis of acute ischemic stroke
title: Very-Low-Field MRI for the Diagnosis of Acute Stroke

brief_summary:
This study is testing whether the JStop™ Hemostatic Device can safely and quickly stop moderate to severe nosebleeds (epistaxis) in adults treated in the emergency department. JStop is a balloon device placed in the nose that applies gentle pressure to stop bleeding, similar to nasal packing and balloon devices already in use.

About 50 adults who come to the Morristown Medical Center Emergency Department with a nosebleed that needs nasal packing will be treated with JStop. The main question is whether the device stops the bleeding within 10 minutes without the need for other packing. The study will also look at side effects, pain, how easy the device is to place and remove, and whether bleeding comes back. Participants will be seen 2 to 4 days after treatment and called at one month to check on their recovery.
primary_outcomes: Number of Participants Achieving Hemostasis Without Alternative Nasal Packing or Balloon Tamponade
title: Safety and Feasibility of the JStop™ Hemostatic Device for Nosebleeds in the Emergency Department

brief_summary: Our accumulating evidence indicates that young adults that have been exposed to Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) display both impaired vascular function, poorer cardiometabolic health, and poor sleep. Our data indicate that sleep impairments may mediate the link between ACEs and vascular and metabolic dysfunction. The primary purpose of this project is to determine if cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-i) is feasible for improving sleep in young adults who have been exposed to ACEs and who have poor sleep. Secondarily, we will collect preliminary efficacy data to determine whether CBT-i can improve vascular and cardiometabolic health in this population, as well as perceived stress and anxiety.

brief_summary:
The goal of this clinical trial is to learn if martial arts training helps lower aggression in children with conduct disorder. It will also compare two ways of delivering this training: through virtual reality (VR) headsets and in a traditional gym. The main questions it aims to answer are:

Does martial arts training lower overall aggression in children with conduct disorder? Do the effects last 30 days after the training ends? Researchers will compare three groups to see if the training works. One group will do martial arts in VR. Another group will do martial arts in a gym. A third group will not do any extra exercise.

Participants will:

Take part in 24 training sessions over 8 weeks (3 times a week). Each session lasts 40 to 60 minutes.

Be assigned to one of the three groups by chance (like flipping a coin). Answer questions about their behavior at the start of the study, at the end of 8 weeks, and 30 days later.
primary_outcomes: Total Aggression Score
title: Virtual Reality vs. Gym-Based Martial Arts Training for Aggression in Children With Conduct Disorder

brief_summary:
TB is caused by the bacillus Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which is spread when people who are sick with TB expel bacteria into the air (e.g. by droplet or coughing). About a quarter of the global population is estimated to have been infected with TB. Following infection, the risk of developing TB disease is highest in the first 2 years (approximately 5%), after which it is much lower. Some people will clear the infection. Of the total number of people who develop TB disease each year, about 90% are adults, with more cases among men than women. The disease typically affects the lungs (pulmonary TB) but can affect other sites as well. Passive detection of TB through healthcare facility attendance alone is inadequate to identify all individuals with TB disease. Ongoing case-detection gaps, particularly in vulnerable groups, along with diagnostic delays and continued community transmission, emphasize the need for more active TB case-finding strategies. Systematic screening for TB disease among populations at high risk is a core element of the first pillar of the WHO End TB Strategy, aiming to promote the early identification and diagnosis of all individuals with TB.

This study aims to compare the Cy-Tb test with the IGRA (blood test) to detect TB infection in individuals who are close contacts and household contacts of patients with TB. The study also aims to evaluate the safety of the Cy-Tb test, the costs and benefits of its use, and participants' opinions regarding the Cy-Tb test compared with the IGRA.
primary_outcomes: Positive coincidence rate of Cy-Tb in comparison to IGRA test in identifying TB infection
title: Cy-Tb for Detecting Mycobacterium Tuberculosis Infection in Indonesian Population

brief_summary: The current post-market clinical investigation is designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of Cellbooster Glow (CBG). For this purpose, healthy participants with signs of skin aging in the face will receive a 3-session treatment and will be followed-up over 70 days after the initial injection session. Several objective measurements of skin quality will be performed with different instruments allowing to assess skin wrinkles, elasticity, dryness, pigmentation, roughness, overall inflammation and microcirculation. Subjective clinical improvement will be evaluated, as well as participant and investigator satisfactions. The safety of the injections will be assessed by collecting the Injection Site Reactions (ISRs) and Adverse Events (AEs).
primary_outcomes: Change from baseline recorded at visit 1 (Day -7 to Day 0) of epidermis hydration measured with Corneometer® at Day 42.
title: Effectiveness and Safety of Cellbooster Glow in Healthy Subjects

brief_summary:
The SOLE PURPOSE PILOT will be implemented in participating African Methodist Episcopal (AME) churches in Louisiana using a community-based approach that integrates structured education, standardized foot risk assessment, and facilitated clinical referral.

Eligible participants will provide informed consent and complete baseline assessments addressing demographic characteristics, diabetes history, foot health knowledge, self-care practices, perceived risk, and self-efficacy. Participants will undergo a standardized foot risk assessment that may include visual inspection for ulcers, calluses, deformities, and other abnormalities; sensory testing using a monofilament; pedal pulse assessment; ankle-brachial index measurement when indicated; and evaluation of footwear and relevant clinical history. Screening findings will be documented using standardized data collection instruments.

The educational intervention will consist of three interactive sessions delivered over a 4- to 6-week period. Sessions will address: (1) recognition of diabetes-related foot complications and individual risk factors; (2) daily foot self-examination, preventive self-care, and appropriate footwear; and (3) recognition of warning signs requiring prompt medical attention, healthcare navigation, and self-advocacy. Educational activities will incorporate culturally relevant examples, demonstrations, and opportunities for participants to practice foot care skills.

Participants with screening findings indicating the need for additional clinical evaluation will receive facilitated referrals through a coordinated patient navigation process. Referral urgency will be determined by the clinical findings and established referral procedures. Patient navigators will assist with care coordination, appointment scheduling, identification of barriers to care, and follow-up to document referral outcomes.

Participants will be followed for three months after enrollment. Follow-up assessments will document completion of recommended foot evaluations, changes in foot health knowledge and self-care behaviors, self-efficacy, and referral outcomes. Implementation measures will include recruitment and participation, intervention delivery, fidelity to study procedures, participant acceptability, and adoption within participating church settings.

Study data will be collected using standardized instruments and managed according to approved institutional research procedures. Descriptive analyses will characterize participant demographics, baseline foot risk, intervention participation, screening findings, and referral outcomes. Exploratory analyses will examine changes in participant-reported measures and the proportion completing recommended clinical evaluations. Implementation findings will be used to identify operational barriers, facilitators, and considerations for future program refinement and scale-up.
conditions: Foot Ulcer Due to Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
interventions: SOLE PURPOSE Church-Based Foot Health Intervention
primary_outcomes: Proportion of Participants Completing a Guideline-Concordant Foot Evaluation

brief_summary:
In this open label phase I/II safety and feasibility study, the investigators use milk plasma, which is filtered breast milk from which fats and cells have been removed. Milk plasma contains substances such as proteins, milk vesicles, and fatty acids, that may help protect the brain and support recovery.

These substances can reach the brain directly through the nose. Studies in animals and early studies in newborn children suggest that breast milk administered through the nose may reduce inflammation and may help brain recovery. The investigators think milk plasma may work even better because it is filtered and can reach the brain more easily, but this is still uncertain.

So far, no harmful side effects were found with the use of breast milk through the nose. Because milk plasma through the nose has not yet been studied in babies with PHVD in the Netherlands, in this study investigators are focusing on safety and how well the treatment is tolerated in these patients. In addition, the researchers want to explore if the milk plasma has an effect on the brain. This is done by measuring certain factors in the cerebrospinal fluid and blood.
primary_outcomes: Safety of intranasal milk plasma administration
Feasibility of intranasally administering fresh milk plasma

brief_summary:
The goal of this observational study is to learn how treatment with incretins, such as semaglutide and tirzepatide, affects muscle mass, muscle strength, and physical function in people with overweight or obesity.

The main questions this study aims to answer are:

* What is the composition of weight loss during incretin treatment?
* What is the composition of recurrent weight gain after stopping incretin treatment?

An additional question this study aims to answer is:

\- How do muscle strength and physical function change during and after incretin treatment?

Two groups of patients will be included: patients who start with incretin therapy for overweight/obesity and patients who stop incretin therapy for overweight/obesity.

Participants who start incretin treatment will have measurements before starting treatment, after six months, and after twelve months or when treatment is stopped. Participants who stop incretin treatment will have measurements before stopping treatment, after six months, and after twelve months or before restarting treatment.

Measurements include:

* Height, length, waist circumference
* Body composition measured with InBody, with a Dual-Energy X-ray Absorptiometry in a subgroup of the participants
* Muscle strength tests
* Physical function tests
* Blood samples to asses metabolic health
* Physical activity measured with an activity monitor (ActivPAL)
* Questionnaires about health, incretin treatment, physical activity, and diet

No treatment or medication will be given as part of the study. Participants will receive incretin treatment as part of their usual care.
primary_outcomes: The composition of weight loss during treatment
The composition of recurrent weight gain after cessation of treatment
title: The Impact of Incretins on Fat-free Mass, Muscle Strength and Functional Capacity

brief_summary:
For safety considerations and to ensure the effectiveness of physical activity within a rehabilitation programme, it is important to establish an appropriate exercise intensity to achieve the programme's objectives. This requires identifying individualised exercise intensity zones that are specifically tailored to each patient, in order to design an effective and progressive exercise training programme.

Exercise prescription is based on four principles: frequency, duration, volume, and intensity. The first three factors are relatively easy to adjust when planning a training programme, whereas exercise intensity is based on a concept that is more difficult to assess and control. On the one hand, exercise intensity is more complex to measure; on the other, establishing individualised reference points and guidelines tailored to each patient is not straightforward.

It is now well established that ventilatory transitions are individualised physiological markers that delineate exercise intensity zones. These transition markers provide valuable reference points for exercise training, helping to ensure that physical activity is both safe and sufficiently intense to induce beneficial physiological adaptations in patients.

Within this rehabilitation context, the aim of the present study is to identify markers of these two physiological transitions during a maximal exercise test conducted under laboratory conditions. The study seeks to identify non-invasive markers related to cardiovascular, respiratory, and motor responses, with a view to conducting similar assessments under real-world conditions in the future. A database has already been established using cycle ergometry (the CAREMO protocol). The next step is to build a new database based on maximal exercise testing, this time using two different exercise modalities: the elliptical trainer and the treadmill. In addition to the new challenge of investigating the second ventilatory transition, the less constrained movement patterns associated with these exercise modalities require adaptations to the analysis methods in order to continue identifying changes in motor behaviour.
primary_outcomes: Inertial Measurement Units
Gas Analysis
Rate of Perceived Exertion (RPE)
Ergometer
title: Observation and Interactions Between Cardio-respiratory and Motor Transitions During Maximal Incremental Exercise Test on Elliptical Bike and Running Treadmill.

brief_summary:
Osgood-Schlatter syndrome is a common cause of knee pain in adolescent athletes. It occurs during periods of growth and is often associated with sports activities involving running, jumping, and repeated knee movements. Pain may limit participation in sports and other physical activities.

This study aims to investigate whether combining proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation (PNF) relaxation techniques with a progressive rehabilitation exercise programme is more effective than progressive rehabilitation exercises alone in reducing knee pain and improving knee range of motion in adolescent athletes with Osgood-Schlatter syndrome.

Twelve adolescent athletes with Osgood-Schlatter syndrome were allocated randomly into two groups. The first group received PNF hold-relax techniques targeting the quadriceps and hamstring muscles, together with a progressive rehabilitation exercise programme. The second group received the progressive rehabilitation exercise programme alone.

Both groups participated in rehabilitation sessions three times per week for 12 weeks. Knee pain and range of motion were assessed before the intervention, after 6 weeks, and after 12 weeks.

The study will compare changes in pain and knee mobility between the two groups to determine whether adding PNF relaxation techniques provides additional benefits to progressive rehabilitation exercises. The findings may help inform rehabilitation approaches for adolescent athletes with Osgood-Schlatter syndrome.
primary_outcomes: Pain intensity measured using the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS)
title: PNF Plus Progressive Rehabilitation for Adolescent Athletes With Osgood-Schlatter Syndrome

brief_summary: Young adults with cancer experience more loneliness than their non-cancer peers or older cancer survivors. brief_summary:
Esophagogastric junction outflow obstruction (EGJOO) can make it difficult for food to pass from the esophagus into the stomach. Some people improve without a procedure to treat the obstruction, while others have persistent swallowing difficulties and may need further treatment.

The O-FLIP study tests whether measurements taken during an endoscopy with a tool called EndoFLIP can help doctors choose an initial treatment for adults with EGJOO. The main outcome is improvement in swallowing symptoms three months after initial management. The study will also track how long improvement lasts and how many participants need further treatment over one year.
primary_outcomes: Proportion of Participants With Clinical Response at 3 Months
title: EndoFLIP-Guided Initial Management of Esophagogastric Junction Outflow Obstruction
